paper_topic: Adaptive Rank Allocation framework and the RaNA adapter, generalizing neuron-adaptive compute methods to operate on arbitrary linear layers via low-rank decomposition + dynamic masking

nodes.text: As Large Language Models (LLMs) have grown in popularity and size, they have begun consuming a non-trivial amount of compute and time for training and inference (Kim et al. (2023), Pope et al. (2022)).
nodes.display_label: LLMs grow in size and compute cost

nodes.text: Adaptive compute methods seek to speed up the inference stage of Transformers (Vaswani et al. (2023)), the de facto LLM architecture, by identifying and avoiding redundant computations to save I/O and floating-point operations (FLOPs).
nodes.display_label: Adaptive compute methods speed up inference

nodes.text: Commonly, these methods apply neuron adapters to the Multi Layer Perceptron (MLP) layers of the Transformer architecture, which dynamically ignore neurons depending on the input of the layer (Lee et al. (2024), Mirzadeh et al. (2023), Liu et al. (2023) Zhang et al. (2024)).

Utilizing these adapters leads to inference speedups, as the amortized time complexity of an MLP layer reduces from O(din ·dhidden ) to O(din ·dadapted ), where din is the input dimension of the MLP, dhidden is the hidden dimension, and dadapted is the average number of active neurons.
For modern Transformer architectures, this results in practical speedups at the expense of negligible model quality decrease for a sufficient amount of average active neurons.
nodes.display_label: Neuron adapters: practical speedup, small quality drop

nodes.text: Unfortunately, adaptive compute methods using neuron adapters suffer from rapid performance degradation in modern Transformer architectures (Figs. 1a, 1c).
nodes.display_label: Rapid performance drop on modern Transformers

nodes.text: Figs. 1a, 1c
We observe this issue arises from the limitations of the neuron-adaptive framework, which enforces dynamic neuron allocation based on activation values.

Concretely, we believe this decline is attributed to this framework's lack of generalization across different layer types, reliance on sparse activation functions, and costly neuron masking techniques.
First, neuron adapters, often tailored to MLPs, can not be directly applied to non-MLP layers, such as the Query, Key, and Value modules of attention layers, which lack neurons.
nodes.display_label: Cannot apply to QKV / non-MLP layers

nodes.text: In addition, these methods frequently depend on activation-induced sparsity, like that attained by ReLU (Agarap (2019)), making them ineffective with non-sparse activation functions like SwiGLU (Shazeer (2020), Zhang et al. (2024)).

Further, while recent approaches like CATS (Lee et al. (2024)) or ReLUfication (Mirzadeh et al. (2023)) attempt to handle non-sparse activations, they inefficiently compute neuron-activations before determining which neurons to exclude.

This is concerning as Transformers architectures like Llama (Touvron et al. (2023)), Gemma (Team et al. (2024)) or Mistral (Jiang et al. (2023)) rely on non-sparse activation functions, which makes sparsity-based neuron adapters ineffective for them, pushing us to rely on more computationally intensive neuron adapters.
To address these gaps in the neuron-adaptive setup, we propose the Adaptive Rank Allocation framework, together with the Rank and Neuron Allocator (RaNA) adapter.
We note that this rank-adaptive framework is a more powerful generalization of the neuron-adaptive one.

Concretely, we devise this framework from the observation that any linear layer can be decomposed into the product of two low-rank matrices and an adaptive router/masker, namely Linear(x) = W x ≈ A(r(x) ⊙ Bx).
Moreover, we develop RaNA in this framework, leveraging specific A and B decompositions and a masker m(x) for Transformer layers, like QKV or MLPs.
nodes.display_label: RaNA: A,B + masker for QKV and MLPs

nodes.text: Notably, unlike neuron adapters, RaNA can be directly applied to any linear layer without relying on activation function sparsity.
nodes.display_label: Applies to any linear layer, no sparsity needed

nodes.text: Further, when used with modern MLP layers with SwiGLU activations, it enables better distribution of compute across the MLP's linear layers.
nodes.display_label: Better FLOP distribution across SwiGLU MLP

nodes.text: We empirically validate the rank-adaptive framework and the RaNA adapter.

We demonstrate that, similar to neuron-adaptive setups, the ranks of the AB matrix decomposition in the proposed RaNA adapters have sparse importances, depending on the input (Figs. 2a, 2b), allowing us to dynamically prune them.
nodes.display_label: Ranks of AB have sparse importances

nodes.text: We also show that RaNA adapters attain the lowest error in MLP layers when recovering the full MLP outputs, outperforming neuron-adaptive methods by 6.7, 18.1 and 7.4 percentage-points on Llama2-7b, Gemma-2b and Pythia-160M respectively.
Further, we show the effectiveness of RaNA in modern Transformer architectures by applying it to Llama (Touvron et al. (2023)) and Gemma (Team et al. (2024)).
Notably, RaNA closes the gap between full-model and adapted-model performance, as it outperforms the state-of-the-art method CATS (Lee et al. (2024)) on multiple compression rates (Tabs. 1, 2).
nodes.display_label: Outperforms CATS at multiple compression rates

nodes.text: Concretely, at a ∼44% FLOP compression rate, RaNA achieves an average improvement of 4 perplexity-points and 8 percentage-points in benchmark accuracy for Llama2-7b, while for Gemma-2b, it improves perplexity by 7 points and accuracy by 5 percentage-points, compared to prior adapters.

Finally, to assess the effectiveness of RaNA's applicability to different types of layers and activations, we apply it to the Pythia suite (Biderman et al. (2023)), a set of varied-sized GPTNeox (Black et al. (2022)) models.
Here we also observe that, when comparing their performance to conventional neuron-adaptive methods, it consistently attains better perplexity and downstream task performance (Figs. 1c, 4).

observations:
The RaNA intro follows a textbook 4-stage method-paper template: (1) Context establishing the LLM compute problem and adaptive compute as a remedy (N1-N2); (2) Prior_Work cluster describing neuron adapters and their MLP-only target with O(d_in d_adapted) speedup (N3-N5); (3) a layered Limitation cluster (N6-N9) listing three specific shortcomings of neuron-adaptive methods — non-MLP incompatibility, sparse-activation reliance, and costly pre-activation compute in CATS/ReLUfication; (4) the Method block (N10-N15) introducing the Adaptive Rank Allocation framework and RaNA, with each component explicitly addressing one of the named limitations.

The Limitation N8 is a parent fork: it expands into three lettered children (N8a, N8b, N8c) that each get distinct addresses-edges from corresponding Method nodes. N14 (any-linear-layer applicability) addresses N8a (non-MLP) and N8b (sparsity), while N15 (better SwiGLU FLOP distribution) addresses N8c (CATS pre-activation cost). N20 (outperforms CATS at compression) addresses N6 (the head Limitation about rapid degradation).

The Result block (N16-N23) is unusually long for an intro — six experimental claims spanning three architectures (Llama, Gemma, Pythia/GPTNeoX) — and largely chains via elaboration since the paper packs multiple distinct empirical claims into this section without explicit discourse markers. One Proof node (P6) anchors Fig. 1a/1c as evidence for the rapid-degradation Limitation.

Anchor paper: none — RaNA builds on the broad neuron-adaptive literature (Lee 2024 CATS, Mirzadeh 2023 ReLUfication, Liu 2023, Zhang 2024) rather than extending one specific anchor paper. CATS is the most prominent named baseline. Topology: N8 is the main fork (3 sub-limitations); N14, N15, N20 each carry an outgoing addresses edge in addition to their adjacency edge, making them mild outgoing-fork nodes.
